Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- 3-day history of frequent watery, non-bloody diarrhea (~6–7/day) with intermittent crampy left lower abdominal pain, initial vomiting (now resolved), subjective fever at onset, reduced appetite, able to maintain oral fluids. Recent restaurant takeaway exposure (~1 day before symptom onset). One child in household had vomiting only. PMH: asthma (well-controlled).  
- Likely diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis. DDx supports viral etiology (e.g., norovirus) as most likely; bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis possible given restaurant exposure. No red flag features reported (no blood in stool, no persistent high fever in transcript).  
- Plan consistent with transcript: Supportive care; no antibiotics at this stage; maintain hydration including oral rehydration solution; acetaminophen (paracetamol) two tablets up to four times daily as advised; rest and time off work for 2–3 days; review if not improved in 3–4 days, with consideration of stool testing if ongoing.

Management Plan
- Oral rehydration: Encourage fluids; consider pharmacy oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte).  
- Symptom relief: Paracetamol two tablets up to four times daily (dose strength not documented).  
- Activity/work: Rest; take 2–3 days off work.  
- Follow-up: If not improved in 3–4 days, return for reassessment; consider stool studies at that time.  
- No antibiotics recommended currently.

Consider:
- Pathology tests as above: Consider stool PCR/culture if symptoms persist beyond 3–4 days (as discussed)

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) – High likelihood: Short-duration watery diarrhea with initial vomiting and subjective fever; household contact with vomiting supports viral spread.  
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne infection (e.g., Salmonella, ETEC, Campylobacter) – Moderate likelihood: Temporal link to restaurant meal; watery diarrhea with crampy pain and early fever compatible; absence of blood does not exclude.  
- Toxin-mediated food poisoning (Staph aureus/Bacillus cereus) – Low likelihood: Restaurant exposure fits, but onset ~24 hours and multi-day course are less typical.
